articles.title: Amazing Grace success thanks to sliding into Hannah Walters DMs, says writer
articles.summary: Daniel P. Lewis's film set in Liverpool snowballed after Hannah Walters agreed to play the lead part.
articles.body:
The star and writer of a new independent film set in Liverpool has said the project would never have happened if he had not sent a "cheeky Instagram message" to Adolescence actor Hannah Walters.

Daniel P. Lewis said he wrote Amazing Grace with Walters in mind and that "it had to be her" for the title role. He described the moment she agreed to take part as a "pinch-me moment".

The film tells the story of Walter, a man on the brink of a mental health breakdown, who forms an unexpected bond with Grace, a volunteer on a crisis helpline.

Lewis said the low-budget production was only possible because Walters helped attract other talent, including James Nelson-Joyce, Sonny Walker, Chanel Cresswell and television director Ruth Carney.

Lewis, who described himself as a "people-watcher", said the story was ultimately "a story of hope and human connection", inspired by his large family and 13 years spent working on the doors around Liverpool.

He said the catalyst for Amazing Grace was seeing bodycam footage posted online of a police officer going to check on a truck driver who had pulled over.

"He [the truck driver] was in a state. He was crying and helpless. The officer realised he needed help and gave him a hug.

Lewis said when he wrote the script he created a vision board for the film, and Walters' picture was on it for the character of Grace.

The self-confessed film buff said he realised he wanted to be an actor after watching This Is England, which Walters starred in.

He enjoyed success with a short film he wrote and acted in called Thomas in 2016, inspired by his late cousin, who had cerebral palsy, and followed it up with Our Kid in 2023, which he wrote and starred in alongside Ricky Tomlinson, Leanne Best, John McArdle and the late Jake Abraham.

Despite that success, he admitted it was a "huge risk" for Walters to take on the project with a relative newcomer at the helm.

Fortunately, Walters said it was a "no-brainer" for her to get involved.

She told the BBC: "The second I read it I was just blown away by the content, by the characters, by the story and its authenticity."

Lewis said that after Walters joined the cast, it "snowballed from there", as she opened the door to other Liverpool talent, including This City Is Ours actor James Nelson-Joyce, Sonny Walker, who starred in Channel 4's The Gathering, and Chanel Cresswell, who appeared in Netflix's The Gentlemen.

Working on a shoestring budget, Lewis said he was grateful to the creative community in Liverpool for "pulling out all the stops" to get the film shot in just 11 days, thanks to help from local media students in the crew and people offering up film locations for free.

"I pulled in so many favours," he said. "I'm so grateful people believed in the film that much."

Joking about the budget, Walters said: "This film was made on a ridiculously low budget - I mean a bag of crisps and a cuddle," she said.

The star and executive producer of the BAFTA winning Adolescence is known for her work to help emerging talent in TV and film.

Together with her husband, Emmy-winning actor Stephen Graham, Walters set up Matriarch Productions to provide a platform for underrepresented voices and stories in the entertainment industry.

She said what the team had achieved with the film, which is showing in cinemas across the UK, was "truly wonderful" and a "testament to Daniel's script".

"It is a very emotive subject, but it also has a beautiful lightness and hope."

Lewis said he had been "overwhelmed" by the response to the film, particularly from people saying it had inspired them to speak out about their mental health, as well as praise from the Samaritans, which supports people in crisis.

"If this film could save a life, I would say it's job done," he said.

Amazing Grace was released in UK cinemas on 6 November.

articles.title: How yesterday's waste is becoming tomorrow's fashion
articles.summary: Brands including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach are among those using recycled materials.
articles.body:
How many clothes, items of bedding and other fabric have you thrown away this year?

While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually – roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers .

The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that.

They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them.

In a warehouse next to the A14 in Kettering, a mountain of crumpled fabric is slowly fed into a machine.

There are dressing gowns, duvets, branded banners and lanyards from events including the Commonwealth Games.

All are made from polyester – the world's most commonly used textile fibre – and all have been thrown away.

Traditionally they would be burned or buried in landfill but Project Re:Claim is trying to change that.

The partnership between The Salvation Army's trading arm (SATCoL) and Plan B Circular operates what they say is the first commercial-scale polyester textile-to-textile recycling facility in Europe – technology adapted from a bottle recycling plant.

The Salvation Army collects the items and those that cannot be reused in their current form are shredded and melted.

Impurities such as dead skin cells and hair are removed and polyester pellets (rPET) are produced which can be used to make new clothes.

"It's the future: using the clothing we have today to make the clothing that we need tomorrow," says Plan B Circular founder Tim Cross.

"We process 500kg of fabric an hour but we could easily scale up if there was demand.

"The problem is encouraging clothing manufacturers to change from using virgin polyester to recycled polyester from old textiles. And to design their new clothes to be easily recycled at their end of life."

"A polyester blazer doesn't need nylon buttons and labels. A sports top doesn't need metal zips. It can all be polyester."

That is important because the plant can only recycle items that are 100% polyester.

Most clothing "is a fibre mix like polyester-cotton, or often three or four different materials," says Majonne Frost, head of sustainability at SATCoL.

Researchers are trialling ways to separate these fibres , but doing it at scale remains difficult and costly, so most of those items are eventually destroyed.

Project Re:Claim says its rPET requires 89% less carbon to make than virgin polyester.

"We send the pellets back to China in what would otherwise be empty shipping containers, and it's spun back into yarn," Cross adds.

"We have the technology but we're way behind with legislation. It absolutely should be driving the way we design and make clothing."

From high seas to high fashion: The students making new clothes from old sails

Designer brings items 'back to life' by repairing

EU rules are already changing and are forcing manufacturers to reduce the waste they produce, their environmental impact, and to make the industry circular.

It must ensure products are not only made from recycled content but are themselves recyclable at the end of their lives.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) says it is "funding the UK Textiles Pact , which is driving ambitious targets to cut waste and increase the life cycle of materials".

In addition, Defra says "a taskforce of experts and businesses is looking at options to reduce waste in homes and businesses and will report back on next steps later this year".

Peterborough-based Gen Phoenix feels global consumer attitudes and legislation are beginning to drive change.

Every year it recycles thousands of tonnes of waste leather into new fabric which has been used by major brands, including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach.

It also specialises in train, bus and aviation seating.

"Jet2 was our first commercial customer, and now we're on one in every five commercial aircraft flying today," says chief executive John Kennedy.

"Our material has similar properties to traditional leather but with an 80% lower carbon footprint and it's lighter. Weight is important for airlines.

"We've saved more than 18,000 tonnes of material from landfill."

Leather is itself a waste product from the food industry, but still much is wasted that Gen Phoenix feels could be salvaged.

"If you think of an animal hide, it's the bits like the neck, the shoulders, the armpits, the belly – bits that don't make good finished leather," says Richard Peace, the company's senior director of research and technology.

The company ships in the waste as "wet blue" – the name given to hides partway through the leather process – from tanneries around the world.

It breaks the leather down into a fibre fluff, which is sprayed on to thin sheets of tissue paper.

The sheets are then sandwiched around a fabric – usually recycled polyester – before high-powered water jets bind all the fibres back together.

Called hydro-entanglement, it forms the new fabric without the need for resin binders, making the new product more easily recyclable.

"The importance of sustainability is seeing a groundswell, both in terms of legislation and consumer attitude - especially with Gen Z coming through," says Kennedy.

"Brands are definitely more invested and are being fairly quiet about the great work they're doing.

"We're continuing to innovate and expand, looking at recycling end process leather too.

"Peterborough is where we do all of our manufacturing and R&D (research and development), and while we may establish other sites, this is where the magic happens."

articles.title: Kent's Defined Wine Ltd turns to carbon capture technology
articles.summary: Ashford-based Cork and Capture says the technology has been developed for the drinks industry.
articles.body:
A Kent winemaker using carbon dioxide capture technology in a bid to be more sustainable says it is "the right thing to do".

Defined Wine Ltd in Patrixbourne, near Canterbury, has installed a unit that captures CO2 produced during the grape fermentation process which can then be reused.

CEO Henry Sugden aims to use the captured CO2 on site and sell any excess to other producers, and claims to be the first UK winemaker using the technology.

He said the company wanted to try it in order to "not increase the pace of climate change". "It's the right thing to do," he added.

Jemima Bland is from Cork and Capture, the Ashford based climate-tech business which has developed the system to make it more compatible with the drinks industry.

"We save breweries and wineries, and other businesses that ferment, money by capturing the CO2 from their production," she said.

"We compress it, purify it and make it available to them for reuse on site."

Although the technology is in use in some parts of the world already, it is unusual, with Cork and Capture aiming to establish networks for capturing and reusing biogenic CO2 within Kent and Sussex before expanding to global markets.

"Here in the UK we've got a relatively new wine sector, and a well-established, up-and-coming small brewing sector," Bland said.

She said the company was hoping to bring "innovation and sustainability" to the industry.

"When we start to compete more with the Spanish and French and wineries that have been making wine for thousands of years, we're bringing the latest technology, the latest innovation and the best possible sustainability," she added.

The UK has experienced carbon dioxide shortages in recent years due to rising energy prices closing fertiliser plants where CO2 is a by product.

The technology also lends itself to beer production, with Hepworth and Co Brewers Ltd in West Sussex already using the system.

"CO2 supply is quite volatile," said chairman Andrew Hepworth.

"It can actually hurt our company if our commercial suppliers aren't available to us. It's far better for us to produce our own and have that security supply."

Alongside the drinks industry, food grade CO2 is used for hundreds of products like promoting the growth of plants in greenhouses, stunning pigs and chickens before slaughter, packaging meats, baby foods, fresh foods and baked products.

It can extend shelf life by preventing bacteria and keep food fresh in transport used in the form of dry ice and snow.

The applications for reduced costs transporting CO2 and using it closer to place of need are "very exciting", Bland added.

articles.title: Krakow shooting suspect has died in hospital, police say
articles.summary: At least six people were killed in the shooting, and three bodies of the suspect's family members were found at their home.
articles.body:
A gunman suspected of killing six people in central Krakow and his parents and sister at their home has died in hospital, Polish police say.

The 24-year-old, who officials said was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies", was injured after opening fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland, on Saturday.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

Krakow police said the suspected gunman died early on Monday morning.

After the shooting, which began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's busy Main Market Square, police identified the attacker as a 24-year-old Polish man but did not confirm his name.

In the hours after the shooting, a minister said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.

Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed in the attack.

Four victims are Polish, while a British national and an Austrian woman were also killed.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.

On Sunday, Polish police confirmed those three victims had been identified as the alleged gunman's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister.

Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.

Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The interior ministry later said they were from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Speaking on Sunday, one of the two surgeons who treated victims on the street after the attack said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.

The two surgeons, who were eating near the Main Market Square when the gunman opened fire, rushed to the scene to treat both the attacker and the two injured police officers.

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible."

"We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."

Pędziwiatr said his colleague, who has been named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most severely injured policeman, allowing time for an ambulance to arrive.

On Sunday it was reported that both injured officers had emerged from comas.

Witnesses who were near the Main Market Square have described their panic and confusion as the attack unfolded.

Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".

She said they "just kept sprinting" until they found a hotel to shelter inside.

Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover".

"I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.

In the wake of the shooting, Poland declared the country would enter two days of national mourning.

After travelling to Krakow, Tusk said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków".

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

articles.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
articles.summary: Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner are reportedly in the frame to replace Daniel Craig.
articles.body:
When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

When will the next James Bond actor be announced?

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline: "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

A handful of actors are thought to have made it to the final screen tests to take on Britain's biggest film role. The three frontrunners are thought to be:

Jack Lowden , 36 - whose credits include Slow Horses and Pride and Prejudice

Josh O'Connor , 36 - The Crown, Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery

Callum Turner , 36 - Masters of the Air, The Capture

Jack Barton , 31 - Heartstopper, SAS: Rogue Heroes

Nicholas Hoult , 36 - About A Boy, Superman

Robert Pattinson , 40 - Twilight, The Batman

Paul Mescal , 30 - Normal People, Gladiator II

But remember, Craig was a surprise choice in 2005, so don't bet against a wildcard candidate whose name has not yet been widely reported.

When will the next Bond film be released?

The film is expected to go into production in 2027, before its release in 2028. No exact dates have been announced.

Film schedules can be notoriously fluid, but it's clear that development is well under way, with the director and writer already in place.

It will be the 26th film in the official film series, but the title has not yet been confirmed.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve , known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight , known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971

George Lazenby starred in just one Bond film, in 1969

Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985

Timothy Dalton starred in two Bond films, in 1987 and 1989

Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002

Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

What are the other James Bond films, in order?

If you discount the films not in the official series, there have been 25 Bond films in total. In order, they are:

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.

articles.title: El Niño pushes world towards record heat as COP31 opens
articles.summary: Scientists are predictng this could be the hottest year on record as the COP31 climate summit opens.
articles.body:
The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.

The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.

Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.

The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.

"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."

On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service confirmed that October was the hottest on record.

But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.

The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday , and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.

It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".

The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.

At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.

"No single COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality," Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, is expected to tell governments on the opening morning.

But he will add "the urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth."

Last month the UK defence secretary warned the public and businesses to think about how they would cope with increasing natural disasters, including stockpiling food.

Wes Streeting pointed to wildfires this summer and record heat, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change , as well as increased risk of flooding this winter as a result of El Niño.

Stephen Belcher, chief scientist at the Met Office, told BBC's Panorama: "We're designed for a climate of the 20th century that we don't live in any longer, so it's going to change all aspects of our lives."

The additional greenhouse gases being added to the atmosphere have trapped additional heat and about 90% of that has been absorbed by the oceans.

That's where El Niño comes in, said Saulo. "It doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release."

This natural climate pattern is pushing global temperatures even higher.

The world is currently on track for 2.8C of warming above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century - all but guaranteed to exceed the goal of 1.5C set under the Paris Agreement to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

Countries will negotiate for two weeks with leaders, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham, attending the conference this week.

Previous climate summits have yielded new targets for countries to follow on cutting fossil fuels, increasing money for developing countries and protections for forests.

Although emissions continue to increase, countries have also made significant progress in increasing renewable energy capacity. The International Energy Agency has predicted growth in the next six years will be 57% greater than the previous period.

Stiell is also expected to say that expanding renewable energy was both a climate and economic solution for recent energy shocks. "Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year."

The Turkish government says it wants discussions this year to focus on a new goal for electrification - moving energy systems away from fossil fuels towards electricity - and cutting waste levels.

But the discussion is likely to split countries.

Early drafts of the EU position seen by the BBC make clear they would only sign up to a goal on electrification if it did not allow countries to meet the target using gas.

"It is important that progress on electrification is underpinned by clean energy sources," it said in a memo to members.

But nations, such as Saudi Arabia and Russia, have previously pushed the interim use of gas as a "cleaner" fossil fuel alternative to coal.

Celeste Saulo of the WMO said she could not offer an explanation as to why countries have previously not reached agreement on certain issues, but said "what I see are the impacts of what this lack of consensus generates with more extreme events".

The BBC understands that the UK government is reluctant to set any new goals at COP31 and thinks the focus should be on achieving existing agreements.

But, on Monday it was reported that the UK government's electric vehicle (EV) targets are expected to be reduced in a move that risks the country's long-term climate goals, according to sustainability groups.

And in September the government was criticised by MPs on the International Development Committee for cutting its aid budget meaning it could not fulfil previous climate funding commitments.

Wealthier nations had agreed at previous COP meetings to triple the amount of money going to developing countries to help them adapt to climate change to at least $85bn (£63bn) by 2035.

The latest data from 2024 shows that countries have reached about a third of that figure, but the UN said this week that the current damage from climate change being experienced is "substantial" and much more money could be needed.

But many countries have redirected aid budgets towards defence spending and short-term financial relief for households as gas and oil prices spike following the Iran-US war.

Governments are also expected to use the forum to discuss global AI policy including the growing demand for energy and water resources from data centres underpinning the technology's rollout.

articles.title: Kenya seize 454kg of methamphetamine in drug crackdown
articles.summary: Kenyan police said investigations started after a key suspect was arrested in Tanzania last week.
articles.body:
Kenyan police have seized 454kg (1,000lb) of methamphetamine worth an estimated $27m (£20m) in an operation targeting international drug trafficking networks.

Three suspects, two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested at the Kenyan coast following an intelligence-led operation involving Kenyan anti-narcotics officers and their Tanzanian counterparts.

Police said the investigations began after a key suspect was arrested in Tanzania last week and handed over to Kenyan authorities at the border.

Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a harmful illegal synthetic drug that is highly addictive and can lead to severe psychosis, heart attack or stroke.

The suspect, who was allegedly linked to a separate seizure of 250 kg of suspected methamphetamine and cocaine in Tanzania, led officers to a location in Msambweni on the Kenyan coast, where the drug haul was discovered.

Police made further arrests at the site and seized two motor vehicles and a motorcycle.

The four suspects are currently in custody and due to be arraigned in court, while the recovered narcotics and the seized items are being kept as exhibits.

The police say the operation remains ongoing and urged members of the public to to share information that will help tackle drug trafficking.

Last month, Deputy President Kithure Kindiki declared illicit alcohol and drug abuse among top threats to the Kenya's future.

He warned that the government would introduce tougher laws and intensify nationwide operations to deal with the menace.

In a separate operation last month, authorities destroyed more than a tonne of methamphetamine from a consignment intercepted last year by the Kenyan navy about 630km (391 miles) off the Mombasa coast.

The Institute for Security Studies, a think-tank, has warned of a shift in East Africa's role in international drug trafficking role.

It says the region's coastline is increasingly becoming not just a transit route for drugs destined for other markets but also an entry point for manufactured drugs intended for local consumption.

articles.title: Canary Islands: 34 dead after migrant boat sinks off Senegal en route to Europe
articles.summary: The Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands remains dangerous for migrants seeking a better life
articles.body:
At least 34 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports, citing an official source.

The Interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.

The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all the bodies recovered so far were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.

In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.

"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.

The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.

Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.

Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.

Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.

Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.

More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.

The Canary Islands have become a major entry point into Europe for migrants and refugees making the dangerous Atlantic crossing from West Africa.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.

Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.

The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.

In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

articles.summary: Russia exploited violent riots in France to spread fake claims about migrant assaults and terrorist attacks, seeking to fuel anti-immigration sentiment,
articles.body: Russia exploited violent riots in France to spread fake claims about migrant assaults and terrorist attacks, seeking to fuel anti-immigration sentiment, deepen social divisions and undermine President Emmanuel Macron's government.According to an internal European Union assessment reviewed by Reuters, a covert Russian-linked network known as Operation Overload circulated fabricated videos impersonating western media outlets to exploit the unrest. The report found that the operation sought to portray French leadership as weak and increasingly authoritarian.The assessment, which covered October 7 to 21, found no evidence that Russia or any other foreign actor had instigated or escalated the protests. Instead, it identified an attempt to capitalise on the unrest after it began, using disinformation to amplify existing political and social tensions.The network circulated fabricated reports claiming that migrants had raped protesters and that terrorist attacks were imminent. By presenting these claims through videos resembling reports from established western media organisations, the operation sought to make false information appear credible and encourage public distrust of French authorities.The EU assessment said Russia sought to "depict the French leadership as weak and increasingly authoritarian". It also highlighted how such campaigns exploit domestic instability to fuel fear, division and distrust in democratic institutions.MAGA-linked and Israeli accounts generated millions of viewsA separate assessment by France's foreign ministry examined the reach of social media narratives pushed by Russian, Israeli-linked and MAGA-linked accounts during the unrest. It found that the 10 most-viewed posts on X from accounts associated with pro-Russian circles received 2.8 million views between October 16 and 18.The reach was significantly higher for accounts linked to the US MAGA movement and Israeli officials, media outlets and influencers. The 10 most-viewed MAGA-linked posts generated more than 49 million views, while the corresponding Israeli-linked posts received more than 35 million views during the same period.These accounts pushed narratives associating the unrest with migration and radical Islamism, according to the French assessment. However, the figures measured the reach of the 10 most-viewed posts in each category and did not establish coordination between the different groups.French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the threat of foreign information manipulation on October 21, although he said there had been no visible foreign interference behind the protests.Russian foreign ministry Maria Zakharova had previously rejected French allegations of Russian disinformation, accusing French authorities of using such claims to manipulate public opinion.Operation Overload has targeted western institutions since 2023The EU assessment identified Operation Overload as a Russian-linked information operation that has been active since September 2023. It targets western public figures, institutions and media organisations to discredit them and promote narratives aligned with Russian interests.The network uses several techniques, including impersonating established media outlets, creating fabricated news videos, cloning experts' voices using artificial intelligence, forging newspaper headlines and manipulating photographs.Research by the UK-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) has also documented the network's activities, describing it as a persistent, high-volume Russian information operation.The operation has repeatedly shifted its focus between countries, exploiting political controversies, public protests and other major developments to spread misleading narratives.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2016, a Mumbai businessman with no farming experience lost his first strawberry crop; 10 years later, Ketan Sodha's soilless Mahabaleshwar farm reports 8,000 kg of fruit and Rs 44 lakh in sales
articles.summary: In 2016, Ketan Sodha bought 5,000 strawberry plants from a local farmer and decided to try cultivation in Mahabaleshwar.
articles.body: In 2016, Ketan Sodha bought 5,000 strawberry plants from a local farmer and decided to try cultivation in Mahabaleshwar. He had no farming background, and his first attempt ended in failure. But instead of abandoning the idea, the Mumbai businessman increased his plantation to 10,000 plants the following year and continued learning how to grow the fruit.A decade later, the 57-year-old's venture, Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP, has a soilless strawberry farm in Mahabaleshwar with a capacity of 19,500 plants. The farm has reportedly produced around 8,000 kg of strawberries and generated approximately ₹44 lakh in sales.As reported by The Better India, Sodha's journey into farming began after demonetisation affected his agricultural land business. He had spent years connecting landowners with buyers across Maharashtra, but the slowdown forced him to consider a different line of work.His first crop failed, but the second attempt changed thingsA fourth-generation Mumbaikar from a business family, Sodha had completed his BCom from KC College under Mumbai University. He first became interested in strawberries around 2012-13, when his work took him frequently through the Mahabaleshwar region.Sodha's first year of farming did not go as planned. “The first year actually was a disaster,” he recalled. In 2017, he increased the number of plants to 10,000. The results improved, and he began producing more fruit than several conventional growers in the area who had been farming strawberries for decades.Other farmers began approaching him for partnerships. By 2019, he was cultivating strawberries across nine acres through a partnership. By the 2020-21 season, his operations had expanded to nearly 40 acres across three locations. He was also working with imported planting material and developing his own nurseries.However, increasing production did not solve one of his biggest problems: unpredictable weather.Unseasonal rain repeatedly affected his strawberry cropsStrawberry cultivation in Mahabaleshwar traditionally depends on the region's cool weather. Farmers generally grow the fruit in open fields, which leaves the plants exposed to rainfall and temperature changes.Sodha told The Better India that unexpected rain around November and early December could set the crop back by 15 to 20 days, just when the plants were approaching their peak production period. “You need to recover the crop, take care of it, spray some fungicides, because the unexpected rain creates a lot of nuisance,” he said.The growing season also had a natural limitation. Conventional cultivation largely stopped during summer and the monsoon because of the heat and rainfall.Sodha began looking for a way to control the growing conditions rather than depend entirely on the weather. In 2021-22, he travelled to Italy, Spain, Egypt and Turkey, where he met nursery owners and hydroponic growers. He also consulted experts from countries including Israel, the UK, New Zealand, Australia and the US. However, he realised that farming methods developed elsewhere could not simply be transferred to India.Why he shifted to soilless strawberry cultivationBerry Fresh Agrotech LLP was incorporated on October 14, 2022. The company's soilless plantation began in November 2024. According to The Better India, Sodha leased two acres of land in Mahabaleshwar and built a 1,500-square-metre polyhouse with the capacity to accommodate 19,500 strawberry plants.Instead of growing directly in soil, the plants are cultivated in cocopeat, a growing medium made from coconut husk. This helps reduce the risk of soil-borne diseases associated with repeatedly growing crops in the same field.The facility uses a retractable roof, a misting system and automated fertigation. Fertigation is a process in which water and nutrients are supplied together to plants in measured quantities.The farm also collects rainwater in storage facilities and treats the water with ozone before using it. Sodha explained the importance of controlling water supply and nutrients to prevent plants from receiving either too much or too little. He described the approach as a combination of several changes rather than a single farming technique.Testing 19 strawberry varieties from different countriesBerry Fresh is also experimenting with international strawberry varieties to identify which ones perform best in Indian conditions. According to The Better India, the farm is conducting trials involving 19 varieties from places including Florida, Spain, Italy, Uruguay and Japan. It has also added a variety from the Netherlands.According to a HortiDaily report in April 2026, the farm is testing varieties from the University of Florida, Spanish and Italian breeders, Uruguay's INIA programme and a Japanese programme called Seeds to Plant. The aim is to study differences in yield, taste, disease resistance and fruit quality. A variety that performs well in one country may not necessarily produce the same results in Mahabaleshwar.Sodha wants to identify suitable varieties for Indian conditions and eventually make better planting material available to other growers.8,000 kg of strawberries and ₹44 lakh in reported salesThe current polyhouse has a capacity of 19,500 plants and operates at around 90 per cent of that capacity. According to the production figures shared by Sodha with The Better India, the farm recorded an average harvest of 408 grams per plant for the period from January 2024 to December 2025. Its reported production was approximately 3.2 kg per square metre.The venture has harvested around 8,000 kg of strawberries and generated approximately ₹44 lakh in sales through business-to-business and direct-to-consumer channels. The berries are sold at around ₹400 to ₹600 per kg, depending on the customer and order. Customers are spread across Mumbai, Mahabaleshwar, Delhi, Bhopal, Ahmedabad, Indore, Udupi and Goa.His next plan is a five-acre farm with 2 lakh plantsSodha is now discussing investments for a much larger facility. He is exploring a proposed five-acre farm in Mahabaleshwar with a capacity of at least 200,000 plants. He hopes to use the experience gained from the first polyhouse to expand the model and eventually replicate it in other parts of India where climatic conditions are suitable.His focus is also on extending production beyond the conventional strawberry season. Early harvests before the regular season and fruit availability after other growers have stopped cultivating can offer access to different market windows.The change has also meant a different daily routine for the Mumbai businessman, who now spends much of his time in Mahabaleshwar.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2017, 21-year-old Sophie Turner bought a West London mews townhouse for £2.6 million; nine years later, after two price cuts, the Game of Thrones star is now accepting offers over £1.75 million
articles.summary: Game of Thrones actress Sophie Turner has slashed more than £550,000 off the asking price of her London Townhouse.
articles.body: Game of Thrones actress Sophie Turner has slashed more than £550,000 off the asking price of her London Townhouse. The 30-year-old is ready to bear a substantial loss of over £1 million, having reduced the price in less than five months in a desperate bid to find a buyer, according to the Daily Mail.Turner, a mom of two, was 21 when she bought the townhouse on a private mews in west London, through her acting company for £2.6 million in July 2017. She managed to negotiate a £295k discount after it was struggling to sell, but now it appears that history is repeating itself. She moved back into the house when she returned to London from the US in 2023 after splitting from Jonas Brothers singer Joe Jones, but now it seems she is ready to get the house off her hands.In May 2026, she put the home on the market for £2.3 million but when no buyers came forward, the price was cut to £1,999,950 in September. Just weeks later, she dropped it again, asking for offers over £1.75 million, meaning Turner has knocked a staggering £550,000 off the asking price in just under five months.If the four-bedroom house sells at the new price, Turner will still be losing £850,000. That is without factoring the six-figure stamp duty she would have paid upon purchase, estate agents and legal fees, pushing the real loss over £1 million. Thus, the agents Chestertons have cast the net beyond the UK and invited Chinese-speaking house-hunters to get in touch through the firm's dedicated China Desk.The listing calls the home 'stylish and very well presented' with 'a beautiful, contemporary finish over four floors.' The property is a private mews townhouse in west London, a style of residence rooted in the city's 18th- and 19th-century horse-and-carriage era, when such buildings were used as stables and accommodation for staff behind grand townhouses. Today, these former service buildings have been converted into sought-after urban homes, prized for their privacy and distinctive character.Turner's contemporary four-storey home combines this traditional layout with modern interiors, featuring three bathrooms and a master bedroom that occupies the entire top floor and opens onto a private balcony. Unlike sprawling celebrity mansions, the townhouse makes efficient use of vertical space, offering a more compact but exclusive form of London luxury.Turner, who boasts an estimated £7.5 million fortune, gained limelight due to her role as Sansa Stark in Game of Thrones, where she was paid £ 158,000 per episode. Now, she is all set to be featured in Amazon's big-budget reboot of Tom Raider to be released next year, where the actress will be playing the role of Lara Croft.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision?
